narrative:
The model estimated a 63.0% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, failure was considered more likely than passing, and because your law school admission was tied to this bar-readiness prediction, your application was rejected. This is a probability-based judgment, not a certainty.

The denial was driven mainly by your academic standing in law school. Your third-year class decile was the single most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure; your first-year class decile was the second most influential factor and also pushed toward failure. Both were 1.00, well below the accepted-student averages of about 5.79 and 6.00. In other words, the model treated your relatively low standing in both early and later years as a strong warning sign for first-time bar failure. Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor and, in this prediction, it pushed toward passing, even though your score of 30.50 is below the accepted-student average of 37.18. It was not enough to offset the academic-standing factors.

Next, ask admissions for feedback and focus on strengthening the academic record the model flagged: seek academic advising, consider coursework or bar-readiness preparation, and reapply only with evidence that your law school performance has improved. You may also ask whether contextual information or a delayed application would be considered.
